articles.title: Pentagon rages as Pete Hegseth's pressure campaign on rescued airmen exposed: report
articles.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ignored concerns about leaking classified information by pressuring airmen to do a ' 60 Minutes ' interview, CNN reported. According to a Saturday article , Hegseth and political appointees in his department pressured two crew members of an F-15 to take part in a '60 Minutes' story that will air on Sunday. Ultimately, one airman agreed to the interview while the other declined, according to CNN. The two were shot down over Iran and then rescued in April. Multiple anonymous sources told CNN that Hegseth went as far as meeting with them personally about going on '60 Minutes.' Hegseth ignored concerns from military officials that the interview risked exposing classified details of the rescue effort, three anonymous sources told CNN. The network that runs '60 Minutes' has also recently undergone a notable overhaul and lost many veteran correspondents and producers since conservative Bari Weiss took over as CBS News Editor-in-Chief with the backing of Trump ally and Paramount CEO David Ellison. Two anonymous sources told CNN that political appointees in Hegseth's office were adamant about both F-15 crew members sitting for the interview, which will be part of the Sunday premiere kicking off the new season of '60 Minutes.' After both airmen raised their concerns, Hegseth personally met with them in private and asked whether they wanted to cooperate, sources told CNN. Hegseth's office has been trying to craft the narrative around the Iran war as it has become increasingly unpopular, CNN noted. CNN couldn't identify the two airmen in the interview, as the Pentagon hasn't publicly released their names. The Pentagon also denied the reporting when CNN reached them for comment. "This entire story is a complete lie," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CNN. "The decision to participate in the interview was each pilot's alone." CNN also noted that the major news outlets, including CNN, were eager to interview the pilots earlier this year, but Weiss personally lobbied Hegseth to give the interview to CBS, three sources at CBS told CNN.

articles.title: Trump's 'biggest mistake' spurs immediate panic among Republicans: report
articles.description: In the wake of President Donald Trump's midterm convention , Republicans are sharing their honest thoughts about how it will impact upcoming elections — and they're not happy. In a Saturday report , Politico collected feedback from Republicans, who didn't mind using profanity to describe their worry over what they saw as the "biggest mistake" Trump made at the two-night event. "He said 'I am on the ballot,' which is going to f— us," said a GOP county chair in a region where House races are competitive because of Trump's unpopularity. "People will vote against congressmen and women to get back at Trump." The midterms are less than a couple of months away, and according to Politico, "a swath of GOP lawmakers" are "near despondent at Trump's comments" at the convention. Over the course of two speeches , Trump promised $5,000 "dividends" for a GOP midterm victory in the House and Senate, continued to call GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton ugly, and had voters promise to "cheat like hell." "I'm sure it helps with the base where enthusiasm is low, but it won't help with independent or swing voters," an anonymous House Republican told Politico. "Not sure he offered a vision for the next 60 days," another House Republican said. "Trump's economy is still on a collision course with reality." Others said that while Vice President JD Vance's speech was better, he didn't do much more to help, even as he told a protester to get his "a— over" to Mexico. One GOP operative told Politico that Vance's speech on the second night wasn't bad, but described it as bland and underwhelming. "There was nothing that stood out to me as powerful enough to stand out online," the GOP operative told Politico. "I haven't seen anything going very viral outside of JD blasting the protester."

articles.title: Trump suffers lawsuit defeat after judge slams staffing plan 'pulled from thin air'
articles.description: A federal judge ruled the Trump administration seized control of FEMA and imposed a staffing cut "pulled from thin air." The order was filed Friday by U.S. District Judge Susan Illston, who sits in San Francisco in the Northern District of California. It was a response to a lawsuit filed against President Donald Trump. Illston granted partial summary judgment to a coalition of unions and local governments. They had accused the Department of Homeland Security of stripping the Federal Emergency Management Agency of authority over its own workforce and ordering it to slash staffing by half. The judge found that DHS pushed FEMA to submit a plan cutting its roughly 23,000 employees down to about 11,500 by the end of fiscal year 2026. FEMA supervisors and the agency's own human capital chief had recommended keeping staffing flat or even raising it. Illston was blunt about where the target number came from. She wrote that the figure "appears as if pulled from thin air." The record showed that Karen Evans, who was then FEMA's senior official, submitted the number first and worked backward to justify it. A December planning document said Evans "has tasked me to develop a strategy to cut the FEMA workforce by 50 percent." The ruling also faulted DHS and FEMA leaders for destroying evidence. Illston found that officials deleted messages on the Signal app using auto-delete timers they set themselves. She concluded that Evans "acted with the intent to deprive plaintiffs" of those messages. Going forward, the court will presume the deleted texts would have hurt the government's case, Illston wrote. Illston pointed to another sign of what she called arbitrary decisionmaking. FEMA halted its wave of non-renewals on January 22, only because a severe winter storm was approaching. The judge noted that a storm on any other date would have meant a different set of employees lost their jobs. The judge denied the government's cross-motion. She ordered both sides to meet and confer on the scope of relief and to report back by October 9.
